prompt.en: A planning note says two matched 9 Ah packs in series give twice the voltage and 18 Ah. What error should you spot?

text.en: The voltage would not add in a series string
The ampere-hour capacity of one series string stays at 9 Ah
Voltage can add only when both packs use lithium chemistry
Polarity stops mattering once packs are wired in series

explanation.en: Series wiring adds voltage, but one matched series string keeps the ampere-hour rating of one pack. Chemistry and polarity still matter.

prompt.en: The same battery and DC leads are used, but transmit current is twice the planned value. What should you predict at the radio input?

text.en: The input voltage rises because the battery capacity is being used faster
Only AC ripple changes; DC lead resistance is unaffected by current
The input voltage falls more because resistance drops more voltage at higher current
The fuse current rating should be increased to hold the voltage steady

explanation.en: Internal resistance and lead resistance cause voltage drop proportional to current, so a higher transmit current leaves less voltage at the radio. A larger fuse does not fix voltage drop.

prompt.en: A supply has enough current headroom, so the buyer skips any RF-noise check and assumes the station will be clean. What is the mistake?

text.en: Extra current headroom proves the output voltage will be correct under every load
A linear supply is automatically unsafe because it is less efficient
A larger fuse current rating is the normal RF-noise filter
Load rating and RF-noise behaviour are separate checks

explanation.en: A supply can meet the current requirement and still be noisy. Load capacity, fuse protection, and RF-noise behaviour must be considered separately.
